title: How the Stanford Prison Experiment Worked
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine the Stanford Prison Experiment conducted by Philip Zimbardo in August 1971 in a basement at Stanford University. They cover how guards and prisoners were recruited and set up, how the simulation escalated into cruelty within days, the prisoner breakdown of Douglas Korpi (whom they say faked it), Zimbardo's girlfriend Christina Maslach ending the study after six days, and the methodological problems: Zimbardo acting as superintendent, coaching guards (recording attributed to Carlo Jaffe), no control group, the "prison experiment" newspaper ad, and the later BBC Prison Study. They discuss the shifting interpretations (inherent cruelty, situationist theory, the banality of evil, and coached authority), the link to Attica and the Nazis, and how the experiment is taught. The episode closes with listener mail about yard work.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour dates
segments.summary: The hosts announce upcoming tour dates in Salt Lake City, Phoenix, and Melbourne, then introduce the Stanford Prison Experiment as a famous but flawed psychology study. They discuss the 2015 film version and its portrayal of violence.

segments.title: Setup and recruitment at Stanford
segments.summary: The hosts describe the August 1971 study in a Stanford basement, the roughly two dozen young male volunteers paid per day, and their random division into guards and prisoners. Prisoners were arrested by real Palo Alto police, booked, and taken to a mock jail with prisoners in smocks and stocking caps.

segments.title: Escalation, prisoner riot, and guard cruelty
segments.summary: The study escalates over the first days. Prisoners riot on day two by barricading a door with cots, and guards turn cruel with forced push-ups, sleep deprivation, numbered identities, and collective punishment. A good cell with better food created informant rivalry. Some guards were kind but did not object to the cruel ones.

segments.title: Korpi breakdown and John Wayne guard
segments.summary: Prisoner Douglas Korpi's breakdown after about thirty-six hours is presented as the official finding. The hosts describe guard David Eshelman, who played a cruel role with a fake Southern accent. Eshelman later said he was acting as the job required. The hosts describe how the experiment was presented as showing evil and fragility.

segments.title: Korpi faked breakdown and the study ending
segments.summary: Korpi later said he faked the breakdown to get out, because he had been denied books to study for the GRE. Christina Maslach, Zimbardo's girlfriend, visited, objected to the treatment, and the study was ended after six days instead of two weeks. Hosts discuss prisoners being told they could not leave, and that the safe word was not in the contract.

segments.title: Visitors, parole hearings, and realism
segments.summary: Hosts describe family visiting hours, parole board hearings where prisoners could forfeit pay for release, a lawyer and a chaplain who played along, and Zimbardo's claim that prisoners could leave by saying they wanted to exit. The hosts note that the record contradicts this and that the documentation is incomplete.

segments.title: Methodology problems and the BBC Prison Study
segments.summary: The hosts list methodological flaws: Zimbardo acted as superintendent, Jaffe coached guards to be brutal (the 'pigs' recording in the French film The Birth of a Lie), there was no control group, and the newspaper ad said 'prison experiment,' attracting biased volunteers. They describe the 2001 BBC Prison Study, which had a control and did not produce brutality, and Zimbardo's alleged private letters to journals.

segments.title: Interpretations and legacy
segments.summary: The hosts outline three interpretations: inherent cruelty and fragility, situationist theory and the banality of evil linked to Nazis, Vietnam, and the Attica riot, and a current view that authority can recruit people to cruelty. They note the study is now taught as a demonstration rather than an experiment and that the Stanford ethics board approved it under the rules of the time.

segments.title: Listener mail: beautiful landscaping
segments.summary: A listener from Point Pleasant, Pennsylvania, thanks the show for company while doing yard work, mentioning past episodes, and shares photos.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, point to the website and email, and sign off.
